summary: Discusses converting hosts from the old NCP protocol to TCP, and making Telnet, file transfer and mail available. The aim is a common interprocess communication environment across the ARPA community.

plainLanguage.summary: Everyone is switching to a new set of network rules. This plan explains how to move the main services over so all computers still understand each other.

questions: how did arpanet switch to tcp
what was the role of relay hosts
when did the ncp to tcp transition happen
subtitle: Orchestrating the switch from NCP to TCP/IP across ARPANET

tldr.problem: The ARPANET was designed around NCP (Network Control Protocol), but work on IP and TCP showed they were necessary for interconnecting multiple different networks, not just ARPANET.
tldr.mechanism: The plan designates a deadline of January 1983 for complete conversion, with relay hosts that speak both NCP and TCP allowing different hosts to communicate during the transition period.
tldr.outcome: The plan succeeded in migrating ARPANET to TCP/IP, establishing the unified protocol stack that became the Internet. Relay services phased out as all hosts eventually converted.

today: RFC 801 describes a successful migration that occurred in the early 1980s. All ARPANET hosts did transition to TCP/IP, and the unified protocol stack became the foundation of the modern Internet. Relay services phased out after 1983 as NCP became obsolete.

sections.title: Why TCP and IP Are Needed
sections.content:
The ARPANET had run successfully for over a decade using the Network Control Protocol (NCP) for communication between hosts. However, research on other networks—including satellite and radio broadcast networks—showed that NCP was too tailored to ARPANET. In 1973, work began on the Internet Protocol (IP) and Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) to provide a common communication standard across all interconnected networks.

IP and TCP allow all hosts in a collection of different networks (called the ARPA Internet or Catenet) to share a unified interprocess communication environment. The Department of Defense adopted IP and TCP as DoD-wide standards and began planning a transition. The time had come to deploy these protocols operationally in ARPANET and open ARPANET hosts to networks beyond the original system.
sections.plainLanguage: A new, more flexible set of network rules had been designed to work with many different kinds of networks, not just ARPANET. It was time to switch over.

sections.title: The Transition Strategy
sections.content:
The plan mandates that all ARPANET hosts implement IP and TCP by 1 January 1982, and adopt the principal services—Telnet (interactive login), FTP (file transfer), and SMTP (mail)—by the same date. The goal is complete conversion from NCP to TCP by 1 January 1983.

Since not all hosts could convert simultaneously, the RFC calls for relay hosts that implement both NCP and TCP protocols. These relay hosts support all three services on both protocols, allowing NCP-only hosts and TCP-only hosts to communicate during the transition. Initially there would be many NCP-only hosts and few TCP-only hosts, but as the transition progressed, most hosts would become "dual protocol" hosts that run both NCP and TCP.

New RFCs document the protocols and services: RFC 791 (IP), RFC 793 (TCP), RFC 764 (Telnet), RFC 765 (FTP), and RFC 788 (SMTP). These specifications would be published in an Internet Protocol Handbook along with implementer hints.
sections.plainLanguage: Every computer had a deadline to switch to the new system, but relay computers would speak both old and new rules so different machines could still talk to each other until everyone converted.

sections.title: Relay Services for Three Key Protocols
sections.content:
The RFC details how relay hosts would bridge the gap for each service. For Telnet, a user at a TCP-only host connects via Telnet/TCP to a relay host, logs in with a special relay account, and then uses Telnet/NCP on the relay to reach an NCP-only service host. For FTP, the process is more complex: a TCP-only user connects to the relay host via Telnet, transfers files from an NCP-only donor host to the relay using FTP/NCP, then downloads the file from the relay to the local host using FTP/TCP. For SMTP, mail relay hosts accept SMTP messages from TCP-only hosts and forward them to NCP-only hosts using either SMTP/NCP (if the destination host supports it) or the older FTP/NCP mail procedure. A special syntax like "user.host@forwarder" allows NCP-only mail systems to route messages through relay hosts to TCP-only destinations.

To maintain reliability and avoid overload, the plan calls for multiple relay hosts, since an overloaded relay would degrade service for all users depending on it. The RFC includes a speculative analysis estimating that as most hosts became dual-protocol, the load on relay hosts would peak in mid-1982 then decline as more hosts migrated to TCP-only.
sections.plainLanguage: Relay computers acted as translators, sitting in the middle between the old and new systems, letting them talk to each other. Different services needed different relay procedures—like postal workers handling mail, file transfers, or phone calls differently.

sections.title: Transition Milestones
sections.content:
The RFC sets a specific timeline. By January 1982, the last NCP-only host would begin conversion, SMTP mail relay service would go into operation, and most hosts would be TCP-capable. By July 1982, most hosts would use TCP-based services. By November 1982, the last conversion would be complete. By 1 January 1983, all hosts would be TCP-capable and use TCP-based services, NCP would be removed from service, and all relay services would end.

Some milestones were already in progress or completed by November 1981 when the RFC was published: some hosts had TCP capability and used TCP services, the first TCP-only host was operational, relay accounts were available to qualified users, and an experimental mail relay using the prototype MTP protocol was running.
sections.plainLanguage: The plan set specific dates: everyone had to start switching by January 1982, and all the old protocol had to be gone by January 1983. Different services would transition at different times.

sections.title: Implementation Challenges
sections.content:
The RFC identifies several critical issues implementers would face. Name tables (the systems that map host names to addresses) would need to grow substantially and possibly track which protocols each host supported. Mail programs would need to be updated to use SMTP, possibly requiring new command syntax to specify relay hosts. The IP and TCP protocols themselves would require continuing optimization and tuning as they moved into production use.

The RFC explicitly warns against implementation shortcuts. It lists common pitfalls from earlier implementations: IP implementations that did not verify checksums, did not reassemble fragments, used static routing, did not process options, or did not report errors properly. TCP implementations failed to verify checksums, reorder segments, protect against "silly window syndrome," process options, or report errors. These mistakes must not be repeated.

Ongoing development of internet gateways was essential, with attention needed on congestion control via ICMP, intelligent use of connected networks, adequate buffering, and fault isolation instrumentation. The RFC notes that work on existing gateways in early 1982 and improved hardware-based gateways in late 1982 would help address these issues.
sections.plainLanguage: Implementers had to be careful: computers needed better address books, mail programs needed new features, and the network hardware (gateways) needed to be upgraded. The RFC warned against cutting corners—past implementations had skipped important checks and broken in real deployments.
